intro: Glasgow's remarkable trees are civic rather than wild. A 450-year-old sycamore survived a 2025 hurricane, an oak was planted in 1918 as a suffrage protest turned permanent, and an ash on Argyle Street arrived as a seed in holiday primroses. A short trip out, the Wallace Yew stands in Elderslie, the pollarded oaks of Chatelherault's medieval hunting park include one dated to around 1440, and two yews at Motherwell's Dalzell Estate have been measured at nearly 30 metres. Most are free to see; Finlaystone, home of a yew tied to John Knox, charges admission.
meta_description: Glasgow's remarkable trees: the Darnley Sycamore, the Suffragette Oak, Chatelherault's medieval oaks and the Dalzell yews. 10 trees, how to reach each.
question_meta: The Darnley Sycamore, 450 to 500 years old and linked to Mary Queen of Scots, is Glasgow's oldest tree, its trunk still standing after 2025 storm damage.
question_answer: Glasgow's oldest tree is the Darnley Sycamore, estimated at 450 to 500 years old, standing on the southern edge of the city near Darnley Primary School. Storm Eowyn tore away roughly half its crown in January 2025, but council inspectors found the trunk sound and expect it to survive for decades yet.
question_context: Darnley takes its name from the personal name behind the district, which pre-dates the sycamore by centuries, but by the time Mary Stuart is said to have sat beneath it in 1565, both name and tree were already established features of the countryside south of Glasgow. The city grew out to meet the tree rather than the other way round; postwar housing now surrounds it on every side, with a fence and small plaque the only markers separating it from ordinary suburban Darnley. It has needed defending twice before: once in the early 1900s, when a resident's complaint kept a new tramline from running through it, and again in 1969, when a Barrhead schoolteacher marched primary pupils out with placards to stop a dual carriageway doing the same. Its most serious threat came from weather rather than planners: Storm Eowyn's 100mph gusts in January 2025 tore away roughly half its crown. Council arborists inspected it by hoist rather than write it off from the ground, found the trunk sound, and expect it to stand for decades yet, its recovery now as much a part of the story as its age.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Glasgow?
faq.a: The Darnley Sycamore, on the southern edge of the city, estimated at 450 to 500 years old. Storm Eowyn damaged around half its crown in January 2025, but council inspectors expect it to survive for decades.

In Kelvingrove Park, near Glasgow University. Suffrage campaigners planted the Hungarian oak on 20 April 1918, days after some British women won the right to vote, and it was named Scotland's Tree of the Year in 2015.

faq.q: Are the King's Park yews open to the public?
faq.a: Yes. The 88 yews stand in King's Park, a Glasgow City Council park on Aikenhead Road that has been open and free since the estate was gifted to the city in 1930.

faq.q: Can you visit Holmwood's giant redwoods for free?
faq.a: Yes. The grounds of Holmwood House in Cathcart are free to walk; only the Alexander 'Greek' Thomson-designed house itself charges admission, free for National Trust for Scotland members.

trees.name: The Darnley Sycamore

location.address: Off Nitshill Road, Darnley, Glasgow G53 7RL

trees.story: For an oak or a yew, 450 years would be middle age. For a sycamore, a fast-growing species that rarely lives past 400, the Darnley Sycamore is already exceptional, and Glasgow has nearly lost it more than once. Local legend holds that in 1565 Mary, Queen of Scots sat beneath its branches nursing her new husband, Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, through an illness, a story specific enough that the tree still carries his name four and a half centuries later. In 1969, a Barrhead schoolteacher marched 28 primary pupils out with placards reading 'Save the Sycamore' when council engineers proposed routing a new dual carriageway straight through it; newspaper coverage of the protest changed the road's course instead. Decades later came a stranger threat: Storm Eowyn's hurricane-force winds in January 2025, which tore away roughly half its crown and left neighbours fearing the worst. Glasgow City Council sent an arborist up on a hoist rather than write the tree off from the ground, and found the trunk sounder than photographs of the wreckage suggested. Officials now expect decades more from it, with unsafe limbs removed and the rest left to regrow. What remains today stands fenced and plaqued on a housing estate that grew up entirely around it, the only visible trace of the countryside Darnley once was.
trees.access: Free, open access, fenced but publicly visible year-round
trees.transport: Priesthill & Darnley railway station, then a walk through the housing estate; local buses run along Nitshill Road
trees.notes: Existence, age estimate and 2025 storm damage confirmed independently by STV News, Forestry Journal and the Wikipedia entry citing multiple press sources; the Ancient Tree Inventory (treeId 145911) corroborates the ancient/heritage classification and gives the surveyed grid reference used for coordinates here. Long-term survival remains genuinely uncertain: a January 2025 council statement described the tree as sound and expected to live decades, but an August 2025 Ancient Tree Inventory visitor comment notes a further limb loss and the database itself lists living status as 'Unknown'. The 1969 dual-carriageway protest, including the teacher's and school's names, is sourced to one detailed local-history blog citing a 1969 Daily Record report; not independently re-confirmed elsewhere, so treated as likely but not fully corroborated. Photo viewed directly 2026-07-31: a large, unmistakable tree with autumn-gold foliage fills the frame behind a protective iron fence on a grass verge, daylight, colour, well framed. Approved.

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fence and plaque around it and a crown still recovering from Storm Eowyn, which tore away about half of it in 2025. It stands off Nitshill Road, Darnley.

trees.name: The Suffragette Oak

location.address: Kelvingrove Park, near Glasgow University, Glasgow G12

trees.story: Not every remarkable tree here began as a sapling nobody thought twice about. This one was planted as a protest made permanent: on 20 April 1918, days after the Representation of the People Act gave some British women the vote for the first time, suffrage campaigner Louisa Lumsden planted a Hungarian oak in Kelvingrove Park on behalf of the Glasgow Society of Women's Suffrage, the Scottish Universities Suffrage Union, the Women's Freedom League and the United Suffragists, groups that had spent years disagreeing on tactics and, for one afternoon, planted a tree together instead. The Women's Committee of Glasgow City Council added a plaque in 1995 on International Women's Day, and in 2015 the Glasgow Women's Library campaigned it to a public vote as Scotland's Tree of the Year, beating five other historic finalists. Storm Ophelia found it in October 2017, stripping around a third of its canopy and tearing its trunk; council arborists reduced its height and rebalanced the crown to save it rather than remove it, and the timber that came down was carved into earrings, coasters and trinket boxes sold by the Women's Library. Now well over a century old and visibly reshaped by that storm, it stands a short walk from Glasgow University, one of the few trees in Britain planted specifically to mark a fight for the vote rather than a coronation or a laird's coming of age.
trees.access: Free, open access, Kelvingrove Park (open daily)
trees.transport: Kelvinhall or Kelvinbridge subway station, short walk through the park
trees.notes: Planting date (20 April 1918), organisers, 1995 plaque, 2015 Tree of the Year win and 2017 Storm Ophelia damage independently confirmed across Wikipedia, BBC News and the Institute of Chartered Foresters. Coordinates from Wikipedia's article-specific geotag, consistent with the Geograph photo's caption placing the tree near Glasgow University in Kelvingrove Park.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a crown reduced and rebalanced after Storm Ophelia tore it in 2017, and a 1995 plaque at its base. It stands in Kelvingrove Park, near Glasgow University.

best_time.label: late October, when the Suffragette Oak turns russet and yellow in Kelvingrove Park

trees.name: The King's Park Yews

location.address: King's Park, Aikenhead Road, Glasgow G44

trees.story: Most of the ancient-looking yews scattered through Britain's churchyards got there because someone wanted shade over graves. These 88 got here because a Glasgow merchant who had made his fortune in the West Indies trade wanted his new estate to look established. When architect David Hamilton laid out the grounds of Aikenhead House for its owner, John Gordon, in the early 1800s, he planted a formal grove of yews on rising ground east of the mansion, then a second, larger avenue of them a little later in imitation of the first. A specialist survey of the site in 2021 confirmed what the difference in trunk girth already suggested: the smaller eastern grove of 22 trees is measurably older and larger than the 66 planted afterward, some girthed at over four metres. The mansion the yews were planted to flatter had itself replaced an even older house on the same spot, one built for a 17th-century Lord Provost of Glasgow that burned down long before. Aikenhead House passed out of private hands in 1930, when developer Sir John MacTaggart gave the house and its 68 acres of parkland to the city as King's Park. The yews needed no care to survive that change of ownership: they simply kept growing, dark and unhurried, while the mansion around them changed hands, uses, and eventually postcodes.
trees.access: Free, open access, King's Park (Glasgow City Council park, open daily)
trees.transport: King's Park railway station (Cathcart Circle Line), short walk
trees.notes: The two groves (22 and 66 yews) and their relative ages by girth are documented by the Ancient Yew Group's dedicated site survey, visited October 2021, cross-checked against Friends of King's Park's own history page for the Aikenhead House ownership timeline and 1805-1823 landscaping dates. No precise planting date exists for either grove, only the estate's documented landscaping window, so the age range is an estimate rather than a recorded figure. Coordinates are the Ancient Yew Group's own GPS reading for their tagged specimen in the older east grove; the entry represents the wider two-grove planting of 88 trees, not a single named tree, in the same way other ensemble entries on this site are pinned to one representative point.

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise the older grove by trunks over four metres round, planted first on rising ground east of the mansion site, before a second larger avenue followed. They stand in King's Park, Aikenhead Road.

trees.name: Holmwood's Giant Redwoods

location.address: Holmwood House, 61-63 Netherlee Road, Cathcart, Glasgow G44 3YU

trees.story: Alexander 'Greek' Thomson's Holmwood is famous for its architecture, a villa modelled so closely on classical Greek temples that its own guidebooks call it his masterpiece, and for years little attention went to what was actually growing in its garden. That changed when the National Trust for Scotland's PLANTS project, a survey set up to catalogue what its properties' grounds actually contain rather than assume the historical record already covers it, worked through Holmwood's parkland and found two Giant Redwoods the trust's own records had barely registered, plus a Himalayan deodar cedar keeping them company. At around a century old, both sequoias are younger than the villa itself, planted well after paper magnate James Couper commissioned the house in 1857, and younger still than California's oldest specimens of the same species, some of which are pushing 3,000 years and eighty metres tall. Glasgow's pair share the same silhouette in miniature: a straight, buttressed trunk and soft, rope-like bark that a curious visitor can press a thumb into without hurting the tree. Whoever planted them was following a very Victorian fashion; seed brought back from California's Sierra Nevada groves after 1853 turned half of aspirational Britain's gardens into pocket-sized redwood forests, and Holmwood's pair survived to become, by complete accident of record-keeping, one of the last things about the estate anybody thought to write down.
trees.access: Free, grounds open to walk daily; the house itself charges admission (National Trust for Scotland, members free)
trees.notes: Both National Trust for Scotland 'PLANTS project' stories independently describe the two giant redwoods and the accompanying deodar cedar, discovered/catalogued during the project's site survey, and give the approximate age as about 100 years; no more precise planting date is recorded by the source. Coordinates are Holmwood House's general grounds point (5 acres), not a surveyed position for either specific tree within the garden.
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for two redwoods with a Himalayan cedar beside them, straight buttressed trunks in soft rope-like bark you can press a thumb into. They stand in Holmwood's parkland, younger than the house.

trees.name: The Argyle Street Ash
trees.story:
The only tree on Argyle Street arrived by accident, in the roots of a primrose. In the 1850s the first residents of a new tenement at Franklin Terrace came back from holiday with primroses for their scrap of front garden, and an ash seed came with them in the soil. Nobody wrote down the year, so its age of roughly 175 years is counted from that story rather than from a ring.

By 1951, when James Cowan described it in From Glasgow's Treasure Chest, it stood 75 feet tall, about 23 metres, and had outgrown the building that planted it without meaning to. It went on to become the first tree in Glasgow to receive a Tree Preservation Order. In 2025 it was voted the UK's Tree of the Year, and in 2026 it represented the country at the European final, finishing twelfth.

The better fact is that it is healthy. Ash dieback has been killing Britain's ash trees for years, and this one still carries more than three quarters of its canopy. The explanation usually given is loneliness. The nearest other ash is over 100 metres away, and a street of warm stone, dry paving and swept-up leaves is a poor home for the fungus. It is a street tree that survives partly because it is on a street. A local arborist, who nominated it for the contest, looks after it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the only tree on Argyle Street, an ash about 23 metres tall that rises above the tenement behind it. It stands in the small front garden strip outside 1223 Argyle Street, at Franklin Terrace.

location.address: Outside 1223 Argyle Street (Franklin Terrace), Finnieston, Glasgow, Scotland

verified_sources: https://www.treeoftheyear.org/previous-years/2026/argyle-street-ash (Tree of the Year entry: around 25 metres tall)
trees.access: Free. Stands on Argyle Street itself, the only tree on the street, in the small front garden strip of a tenement building at Franklin Terrace; visible and reachable from the public pavement, no entry needed.
trees.transport: Kelvinhall or Exhibition Centre subway/rail stations, both under 10 minutes' walk

trees.name: The Wallace Yew

location.address: Wallace Monument and birthplace site, Park Avenue, Elderslie, Renfrewshire PA5
location.neighbourhood: Elderslie (Renfrewshire, about 11 km west of Glasgow centre)

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 2338 (a society record, not a statutory register)

trees.access: Stands in the open grass of the Wallace Monument and birthplace site beside the ruins of Wallace's house; protected by a fence (SYTHI photo 2021), so seen from outside it. No opening hours found; no sign of a gate or ticket in any source. Not verified from OSM (Overpass is dead from this runner).
trees.transport: Day trip from Glasgow. ScotRail from Glasgow Central to Johnstone, four trains an hour, about 14 minutes (ScotRail average), then about 11 minutes on foot east to Park Avenue. Elderslie's own station closed in 1966. Buses also stop at Park Avenue, Elderslie.
trees.story:
Nobody agrees whether the Wallace Yew is seven centuries old or closer to three. Elderslie's legend says William Wallace planted it, or that it grew up alongside him, which would make it about 700 years old. Scotland's Yew Tree Heritage Initiative reports that expert investigation points instead to a planting about 300 years ago, perhaps in the 1760s, when the Wallace estate passed to the Speirs family. Then it argues the other way. Parish records of the 1700s already called it "this ancient tree", and the Statistical Account of Scotland in 1845 thought it "co-eval with, some say older than" the village's Wallace Oak, which fell in a storm in 1856. A 1977 guidebook muddied things further, saying the yew by the house was seeded from an older tree known as Wallace's Yew. Nobody has ever recorded its girth.

What it has survived is less disputed. It was set on fire in 1978. On 12 January 2005 a storm ripped away half the trunk almost to the ground. Since about 2008 a Ganoderma fungus has been at the wood, and the tree is reported to be in decline, regrowing from what is left. Renfrewshire Council took twelve cuttings that year; six rooted, to be planted nearby as clones.

It stands fenced in the grass beside the ruins of Wallace's house in Elderslie, about 11 kilometres west of central Glasgow: roughly a quarter of an hour by train from Glasgow Central to Johnstone, then about 11 minutes on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the iron fence ringing it: a lone yew regrowing from what a 2005 storm left of its trunk. It stands in the grass beside the ruins of Wallace's house, by the Wallace Monument.

trees.name: The Cadzow Oaks

location.address: Cadzow oak pasture, Chatelherault Country Park, Ferniegair, Hamilton ML3 7UE

trees.story:
One of the oaks in this pasture has been dated to around 1440. Historic Environment Scotland, which lists the Chatelherault landscape in its inventory of designed landscapes, describes the Cadzow oaks as pollards so old they are difficult to date at all, and that one date is the firm point in the fog. Parks and Gardens UK repeats it. Most of the others are simply called ancient, and local captions say over 500 years.

They are what remains of the Hamilton High Parks, the medieval hunting forest of Cadzow on the slopes near Cadzow Castle. The oaks are the reason the ground is a Site of Special Scientific Interest. They were pollarded, cut back at head height so they regrew above the reach of grazing animals, and they still stand singly in grazed pasture, which is about as close as Scotland gets to seeing a medieval park the way it was used. Not all of them made it. Historic Environment Scotland records trees lost to intensive farming in the 20th century.

Which oak they are is less settled than you would think. One description of the site calls them pedunculate oaks, another sessile, so we list them as oak and would like to hear from anyone who has looked at the acorn stalks.

Chatelherault Country Park is free and open all year. The oaks were still being recorded by naturalists in September 2026.

official_register.name: Historic Environment Scotland, Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes: Chatelherault (Hamilton High Parks SSSI oaks)

trees.access: Free. Chatelherault Country Park is open all year. The oaks stand in grazed pasture by the park paths near Cadzow Castle.
trees.transport: Day trip from Glasgow to Hamilton. Train to Hamilton Central, then about 2 km by road to the park, so allow for a bus, a taxi or a longer walk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the old pollarded oaks standing singly in open grazed pasture, not in the woodland. They stand on the slope near Cadzow Castle and its earthworks in Chatelherault Country Park.
trees.verify_notes: ENSEMBLE, one place to stand: the ancient oak pasture of the Hamilton High Parks, a medieval hunting park (Cadzow Forest). Historic Environment Scotland (GDL00101): ancient pollarded oaks so old they are difficult to date, one dated to c.1440; Hamilton High Parks is an SSSI for the oaks; some trees lost to 20th-century intensive farming. Parks and Gardens UK repeats the c.1440 date and the SSSI. A South Lanarkshire leaflet and Geograph captions say 'over 500 years' (caption only, not a source). A 2014 blog claims up to 700-900 years via dendro; treat as unverified and DO NOT use. Girth not recorded in any source I could fetch (the Woodland Trust ATI holds girths but is off limits). Species given as Pedunculate Oak by the Commons file description (Rosser1954); the blog says sessile, so species is unsettled: write 'oak (Quercus robur)' with caution or use 'Oak (Quercus sp.)'. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2026-09-06 at the site; Geograph photos 2007 to 2021. No individual named tree; I could not pin one trunk, so the point is the pasture beside the castle earthworks. Geotags of Geograph photos cluster at 55.7575-55.7584, -4.0189 to -4.0196. Scotsman article 'Oaks rooted in 700 years of Scots history' exists but is Cloudflare-blocked (not read). The Cadzow oaks also held Scotland's famous wild white cattle herd (not verified here). Walk: the park path network is the walk; the Avon Gorge is the same park. Writing pass 2026-11-03: species set to Oak (Quercus sp.) as these notes advise (sources disagree pedunculate/sessile). Photo approved after viewing the pixels: one Cadzow oak fills the frame in summer daylight, in leaf, titled as one of the Cadzow Oaks; two small unrecognisable figures at the right edge, outside the centre crop.

trees.name: The Covenanters Oak
trees.age_estimate: not documented, called the oldest living thing in North Lanarkshire

location.address: Dalzell Estate, near Dalzell House, Manse Road, Motherwell ML1 2SD

trees.story:
North Lanarkshire Council, which owns the ground, calls this oak probably the oldest living thing in North Lanarkshire. It is also held together with steel.

In August 2008 heavy rain brought down one of its three great scaffold limbs, and the fall tore the main stem open in a crack running from the ground to about two metres up. A firm of arborists from Perth braced it that autumn. The longer-term repair is still there. Two steel cables with nylon slings hold the crown together, and two steel props stand under it, bolted into concrete pads.

Nobody has given it a published age we can stand behind, and we have not settled which oak it is either. If you know, tell us. The name points to the Covenanters, the Presbyterians who held outlawed services in the open air in the 17th century, but we have not found a source that ties them to this tree, so take the name as a name.

It stands near Dalzell House, on the path between the Japanese Garden and the mansion's main entrance, a few hundred yards of walking. A walking blog updated in 2022 still describes it there. The estate is a free public park, and Jacob and Esau, two exceptionally tall yews, grow in the woods of the same estate.
trees.access: Free public park run by North Lanarkshire Council.
trees.transport: Train to Motherwell, then a walk of a kilometre or more to the Dalzell Estate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the steel cable braces in its crown and the two steel props at its base. It stands near Dalzell House, on the path between the Japanese Garden and the mansion's main entrance.
trees.verify_notes: Council (North Lanarkshire, owner of the ground): near the main house, 'probably the oldest living thing in North Lanarkshire'; age and weather damage, work done to preserve it. Heritage World article: August 2008 heavy rain tore a wound in the main stem when one of three major scaffold limbs collapsed; open crack from ground to about 2 m; Aboretum Internationale (Perth) fitted emergency bracing that autumn, then a longer-term system of two steel cable braces with nylon slings and two steel props bolted into concrete pads. Walking blog (post dated 2020, updated Oct 2022) places it on the route from the Japanese Garden to the mansion, a few hundred yards, calls it a 'mighty tree', so alive as of 2020-22. lifecheck at Dalzell House: RECENT, iNaturalist 2024-01-13 (nearby, not the oak). Pin is the house, tree within a few hundred metres, approximate. Species, girth and numeric age: the only figures I saw (sessile oak, 6.7 m girth, over 800 years, royal deer park of David I) came up in search results from the Woodland Trust Ancient Tree Inventory, which is off limits, so NOT used; the Covenanter story (open-air worship under the oak during 17th century persecution, the Hamilton family hosting) appears in search summaries only and has not been seen on a fetched page: do not state it without a source. No photograph on Commons; Geograph is behind Cloudflare. Photo pass 2026-11-04 (approved): Commons file titled Covenanters' Oak (Geograph import), the propped, hollowed oak fills the frame inside its railing, daylight, in leaf. Camera 116 m from our pin, so the pin is not upgraded.

trees.name: Jacob and Esau, the Dalzell Yews

location.address: Woods below the arboretum, Dalzell Estate, Motherwell ML1 2SD

trees.story:
In 2022 two climbers went up a pair of yews in a Motherwell wood with a tape measure. Jacob came out at 29.8 metres and Esau at 29.5. The Arboricultural Association's magazine, which reported the climb, says Jacob could be the tallest yew in Europe. The record it was set against, a yew at Belvoir Castle in England, stood at 28.4 metres when measured in 1987.

Yews are usually broad, dark and not especially tall, which is what makes this pair odd. They grow either side of a path on a riverbank, at the foot of a bowl-shaped hollow in the woods below the Dalzell Estate arboretum, close enough to count as one stop. Esau is the thicker of the two, though nobody has published its girth. Neither has a published age.

The trees are registered with the Tree Register of the British Isles. We have not found an exact position for them, and our pin marks Dalzell House rather than the trees, so head for the arboretum and go down into the woods below it. The estate is a free public park; the magazine report does not say whether the path to this spot is open to everyone, so if you get there, tell us how you found it.
trees.access: Free public park run by North Lanarkshire Council. The yews stand by a path on a riverbank; public access to that exact spot is not confirmed.
trees.transport: Train to Motherwell, then a walk of a kilometre or more to the Dalzell Estate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a pair of very tall yews growing either side of a path on a riverbank. They stand at the foot of a bowl-shaped hollow in the woods below the Dalzell Estate arboretum.
trees.verify_notes: Treecare / Arboricultural Association magazine (ARB Magazine issue 197, summer 2022, David Treanor, with Mark Foster): Jacob measured 29.8 m, Esau 29.5 m, by tape after being climbed (Foster climbed Esau, Douglas Crawford climbed Jacob); Esau is the girthier, no girth given; 'could be the tallest in Europe'; previous record Belvoir Castle yew 28.4 m (1987). Registered with the Tree Register (TROBI). Search summaries add that the Tree Register called Jacob the tallest known yew and a national champion found 2024 at 29.8 m: only the treecare.org.uk page was actually read, the Tree Register page returned an index, and the Daily Record/Cumbernauld News story 403'd. Treat 'tallest in Europe' as a claim to quote with attribution, not fact. Superlative-collision check needed. Twin trees metres apart: one collectible point. Exact spot not found in any fetched source; pin is Dalzell House, tree within the estate, approximate. No photograph found.

trees.name: John Knox's Yew

location.address: Finlaystone Country Estate, Langbank, Port Glasgow, Renfrewshire PA14 6TJ

trees.story:
John Knox's Yew is not where John Knox stood. Around 1900, during alterations to Finlaystone House, the yew was moved about 30 metres rather than felled, and it survived the move. A tree now reckoned to be somewhere between 400 and 800 years old was shifted across the grounds and kept growing.

The Knox part of the story rests on 1556. In that year the reformer led a communion service at Finlaystone for the family of the Earl of Glencairn, which accounts of the house's history confirm. Tradition adds that he preached under this yew. Some say he planted it. Others say it was already old when he arrived, and Scotland's Yew Tree Heritage Initiative, which classes it as ancient, sides with neither. Nobody has published a girth or a height.

It grows as two stems, and its north-facing side carries a thinner, less healthy crown than the rest, possibly from storm damage since the move. The only photograph we can find was taken in 1981, so we cannot say how it looks now. If you visit, tell us.

Finlaystone is a visitor estate of gardens and woodland run by a ranger service above the Clyde at Langbank. Admission fees and opening times apply, so check the estate's own site before you go.
trees.access: Finlaystone Country Estate, a visitor estate with paid admission and set opening times; check Finlaystone's own site before visiting.
trees.transport: Day trip from Glasgow to Langbank. Train on the Inverclyde line to Langbank station, then walk to the estate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its two stems and by the thinner crown on its north-facing side. It stands in the grounds of Finlaystone House.
trees.verify_notes: Scotland's Yew Trees (SYTHI) lists 55.928582,-4.619781, grid NS 36459 73717, age class ancient 400-800 years, no girth or height (the Ancient Yew Group database also holds no girth). Provenance is debated: some claim Knox planted it mid-16th century, others that it was already old; Knox is said to have preached under it and given communion to the family of the 5th Earl of Glencairn in 1556 (SYTHI; Wikipedia's Finlaystone House article confirms the 1556 communion service led by Knox but does not mention the yew). Moved about 30 m in 1900 during alterations to the house rather than felled and survived (SYTHI), so it is NOT standing where Knox stood in 1556; a presentation by Paul Greenwood (Ancient Tree Forum, seen only in a search summary, PDF too large to fetch) says the same. Condition per SYTHI: north-facing canopy thinner, possibly storm damage since the move. ALIVE: no dated recent source; the only photo is from 1981 and lifecheck is OLD, so flagged. SYTHI text is copyright, do not copy. Geograph subject geotag and SYTHI coordinate agree within about 25 m. Pin approximate (grounds of a house, individual tree not mapped). Superlative caution: do not call it the oldest yew. Photo held (writing pass 2026-11-03): a 1981 slide; the yew is clear in daylight but a group of visitors stands under it, and a 45-year-old picture cannot show the tree as it is now while its survival is unconfirmed. A recent photograph wins.
